segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us also lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles, and run with endurance the race set before us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured a cross, scorning the shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For consider him who has endured such opposition from sinners against themselves, so that you may not grow weary in your souls and lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: for the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and flogs every son he accepts.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is for discipline that you endure. God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you are without the discipline in which all have come to share, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Besides, we had our fathers in the flesh to discipline us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they disciplined us for a few days as seemed best to them, but he does it for our benefit, so that we may share in his holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No discipline seems at the time to be a matter of joy, but of grief; later, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore set straight the drooping hands and the weakened knees,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: watching that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness grows up and causes trouble, and through it many are defiled,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that no one is sexually immoral or profane like Esau, who for a single meal sold his own birthright.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know that afterward, when he did want to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for turning back, though he sought it with tears.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you have not come to something that can be touched and a blazing fire, to darkness and gloom and storm,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and a trumpet blast and a voice speaking words—a voice whose hearers refused to have any further word spoken to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they could not bear what was commanded:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, so fearful was the sight that Moses said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am full of fear and trembling.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused the one who warned them on earth, much less will we, if we turn away from the one who warns from the heavens.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now this “Yet once more” points to the removal of the things that are shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that are not shaken may remain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be grateful, and so serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for our God is indeed a consuming fire.

notes.phrase: the sin that so easily entangles
notes.traditional: the sin which doth so easily beset us
notes.note: The Greek adjective occurs nowhere else in surviving literature before this verse, so its exact sense is uncertain. Most scholars take it as “easily surrounding” or “clinging closely,” which suits the picture of a runner stripping off anything that hampers; “easily distracting” is the reading of one very early manuscript. The rendering here follows the majority view.

notes.traditional: the author and finisher of our faith
notes.note: The first word means a leader who goes first and opens the way for others, and can also mean a founder or originator; “pioneer” (as in several modern versions) fits the race imagery better than “author.” The Greek has no “our”: Jesus is presented as the one who both leads the way in faith and brings it to its goal, not only as the source of the readers’ own faith. “Perfecter” belongs to the same word-family as “made perfect” in verse 23.

notes.phrase: for the joy set before him
notes.traditional: for the joy that was set before him
notes.note: The preposition can mean “for the sake of” or “instead of.” Most interpreters take it as the former: Jesus endured the cross to gain the joy that lay ahead. A minority read “instead of the joy that lay within his reach, he endured a cross.” The same preposition is used in verse 16 of Esau selling his birthright “for” a meal.

The Greek text translated here reads the plural “against themselves,” which has strong support in the earliest manuscripts; other manuscripts, followed by most English versions, read the singular “against himself.” With the plural, the thought is that the sinners’ opposition to Jesus was to their own harm, perhaps echoing the description of Korah’s company in Numbers 16:38. Many scholars regard the plural as the harder reading and are divided over which is original.

The Greek word covers the whole upbringing of a child: instruction, training and correction, including punishment. “Discipline” is used throughout the passage in that broad sense, not as a synonym for punishment alone. The quotation is Proverbs 3:11–12 in its Greek form, whose second line (“flogs every son he accepts”) differs from the Hebrew, “as a father the son in whom he delights.”

The verb ordinarily means “turn aside,” and some take it so here: the lame should not be made to stray from the path. It was also used by medical writers for a limb being dislocated, and the contrast with “be healed” favors that sense, which most modern versions adopt.

The traditional “repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word denotes a change of direction, a reversal. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term. Some scholars think the phrase here is close to a legal idiom, “no opportunity for reversal,” meaning that Esau could not get the decision changed.

notes.phrase: though he sought it with tears
notes.traditional: though he sought it carefully with tears
notes.note: “It” could refer either to the blessing or to the turning back; both nouns are feminine in Greek. In Genesis 27:34–38 Esau weeps and pleads for the blessing, which favors the first, but the nearer noun is “turning back,” and interpreters are divided. The English leaves the reference as open as the Greek.

notes.traditional: the mount that might be touched
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have no word for “mountain” here; later manuscripts add it, probably to match “Mount Zion” in verse 22. The scene is Mount Sinai at the giving of the Law (Exodus 19–20; Deuteronomy 4–5), which the first readers would have recognized from the fire, darkness, trumpet and voice without its being named.

Most versions have “begged that no further word be spoken.” The verb means to ask to be excused from something, to decline or refuse, and it is the same verb used twice in verse 25 (“do not refuse the one who is speaking”). It is rendered “refuse” in both places so that the link the author draws between Israel at Sinai and the readers is visible.

notes.traditional: to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn
notes.note: The word means a festival gathering. It can be attached to what precedes (“myriads of angels in festal gathering”), as here and in most modern versions, or to what follows (“to a festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn”), which is how some editions punctuate the Greek. The sense of the whole is little affected.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and was the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God; “church” now suggests a building or an institution. Nearly all translations use “church,” and readers generally know what it refers to. “Assembly” is used here to keep the first-century sense, which suits this picture of a people gathered at the mountain.

notes.traditional: that speaketh better things than that of Abel
notes.note: In Genesis 4:10 Abel’s blood cries out to God from the ground, a cry usually understood as a call for justice; Hebrews 11:4 says that Abel, though dead, still speaks. The blood of Jesus, pictured as sprinkled like the blood that sealed the covenant at Sinai, speaks a better message. The Greek says simply “than Abel”; many versions expand to “than the blood of Abel.”

The Greek phrase “have grace” was a common idiom for “be thankful,” and most modern versions take it that way. The older rendering, “let us have grace” (that is, hold on to God’s grace), is also possible, since the same noun means “grace” in verse 15.

candidates.reason: Used of Jesus in Acts 3:15; 5:31 and Hebrews 2:10; 12:2, and versions vary between author, founder, prince, leader and pioneer; one choice is needed so the title is recognizable.

The noun and its verb παιδεύω range from training and instruction to punishment (Ephesians 6:4; 2 Timothy 3:16; Titus 2:12; 1 Corinthians 11:32; Luke 23:16), and a consistent policy on discipline/training/instruction is needed.
Frequent across Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation and variously rendered patience, perseverance, steadfastness or endurance; the link with the verb ὑπομένω (“endure”) should stay visible.
Central term across the New Testament that can mean covenant or will/testament (notably Hebrews 9:16–17; Galatians 3:15), so a single policy with defined alternates is needed.
Pervasive word whose senses (grace, favor, gift, thanks) need fixed rules, including the idiom ἔχειν χάριν for “be grateful” as in verse 28.
